firmware.summary: The rover runs its own Wi-Fi network called "Rover-XXXX". It serves a single web page with a touch joystick. The phone sends a drive command about 10 times a second, and the firmware turns it into left and right wheel speeds for the DRV8833. The PWM runs at 20 kHz, uses slow decay, is capped at 75 % duty (about 6.3 V on the 6 V motors at full charge) and ramps up gently. If commands stop for 500 ms, the motors brake and the driver goes to sleep. The battery is read through the 100k/33k divider and filtered: below 6.8 V the red LED comes on as a warning, and below 6.4 V for 3 seconds the drive cuts out. The green LED shows the link state.

pins.note: Held LOW at boot and on failsafe; not a strapping pin

#pragma once
// Pin map for U1 ESP32-C3-MINI-1 on the A1 DevKitM-1 carrier.
// The C3 strapping pins (GPIO2, GPIO8, GPIO9) are deliberately left unused.

#define PIN_AIN1        4   // DRV8833 AIN1 -> left motor
#define PIN_AIN2        5   // DRV8833 AIN2 -> left motor
#define PIN_BIN1        6   // DRV8833 BIN1 -> right motor
#define PIN_BIN2        7   // DRV8833 BIN2 -> right motor
#define PIN_DRV_NSLEEP 10   // DRV8833 nSLEEP, LOW = outputs off

#define PIN_VBAT_SENSE  3   // ADC1_CH3, 100k/33k divider tap

#define PIN_LED_GREEN   0   // D1 green anode via 330R
#define PIN_LED_RED     1   // D1 red anode via 330R

// LEDC channels for the four bridge inputs
#define CH_AIN1 0
#define CH_AIN2 1
#define CH_BIN1 2
#define CH_BIN2 3

build: Install PlatformIO (VS Code extension or `pip install platformio`).
Put a platformio.ini built from platformioEnv in the project root: platform espressif32@6.5.0 (Arduino-ESP32 2.0.x), board esp32-c3-devkitm-1, monitor_speed 115200.
With the rocker switch OFF and the JP1 shunt REMOVED, connect the DevKitM-1 to USB-C and flash it with `pio run -t upload`.
Watch the console with `pio device monitor`. It prints the SSID, the IP (192.168.4.1) and the battery voltage every 2 s.
Unplug USB, refit the JP1 shunt and power the rover from the rocker switch.
test: Run on USB only: JP1 off, no cells and wheels off the ground. The LED should alternate red and green (USB bench mode). The console should read VBAT close to 0 V and nSLEEP should stay LOW, so the motors cannot move.
Join the 'Rover-XXXX' Wi-Fi network (password rover1234) and open http://192.168.4.1. The page should show the voltage and 'no battery (USB)', and the joystick must not move anything.

Put the rover on a stand with the wheels in the air. Fit the cells and the JP1 shunt, then switch on. The LED should blink green, and the console VBAT should be within 0.1 V of a multimeter reading across the pack. If not, adjust DIV_RATIO.

Push the joystick gently forward. Both wheels should spin forward and ramp up smoothly. If one runs backwards, flip INVERT_LEFT or INVERT_RIGHT. Push left and right to check the turn direction. The LED should be solid green while the page is open.
Check the failsafe: while driving, turn the phone's Wi-Fi off or close the browser tab. The wheels must stop within about 0.5 s and the LED must go back to blinking green.
Measure the PWM at full joystick with a scope on the motor terminals. It should be 20 kHz at about 75 % average voltage, around 6.3 V at 8.4 V.

Check the low-battery logic with a bench supply in place of the pack (current limit 1 A). At 6.7 V the LED turns solid red but driving still works. Below 6.4 V for 3 s the motors stop and the red LED blinks fast. Drive stays off until the supply is raised above 7.2 V.
Finally, test on the floor at low speed, then at full speed. Watch that the rover does not reset when motors start or reverse, which would show as the boot banner reappearing in the console.
assumptions: The phone link is the ESP32 acting as its own Wi-Fi hotspot, with the built-in Arduino WebServer serving a touch-joystick page. No phone app or extra libraries are needed. SSID is 'Rover-' plus the last 2 MAC bytes, password is 'rover1234', IP is 192.168.4.1, channel 6.
The page sends GET /drive?x=-100..100&y=-100..100 every 100 ms, even when the stick is centred, so it doubles as a heartbeat. If no command arrives for 500 ms, the motors stop and nSLEEP goes LOW.

Pins come straight from the design: AIN1/AIN2 = GPIO4/5 (left motor), BIN1/BIN2 = GPIO6/7 (right motor), nSLEEP = GPIO10, VBAT_SENSE = GPIO3, green LED = GPIO0, red LED = GPIO1. None of these are C3 strapping pins (GPIO2/8/9).

Motor PWM is LEDC at 20 kHz with 10-bit resolution, in slow-decay (drive/brake) mode. Zero command brakes the motors with both inputs high; asleep means all inputs low. Duty is capped at a fixed 75 % as the design asks; it is not adjusted for battery voltage.
Acceleration is limited to full scale in 250 ms to keep start surges off the 3.3 V rail. Slowing down and stopping happen immediately.
Mixing is arcade style (left = y + 0.6x, right = y - 0.6x), normalised to ±1, with a 6 % deadband.
The right motor is assumed to be mounted mirrored, so INVERT_RIGHT = true. Flip it on the bench if needed.
Battery: VBAT = ADC mV / (33/133), with 11 dB attenuation and analogReadMilliVolts for factory calibration. It is sampled every 50 ms with an EMA filter (alpha 0.1).

Battery thresholds: warning below 6.8 V (clears above 7.0 V). Cut-off below 6.4 V held for 3 s, which ignores short sag when motors start. After cut-off, driving only comes back above 7.2 V, i.e. a recharged pack. Below 3.0 V the board is treated as USB-powered with no battery and the driver stays asleep.
LED states: blinking green = ready but no phone commands, solid green = phone driving, solid red = low battery, fast blinking red = cut-off, alternating red/green = USB-only bench power.
Wi-Fi transmit power is reduced to 11 dBm and modem sleep is off. Desk range is enough, and this lowers both current draw and command delay.
Build is pinned to the espressif32 6.5.0 platform (Arduino core 2.0.x), which uses the ledcSetup/ledcAttachPin API.
The design calls this a 'walking robot' but every block describes a two-wheel rover, so the firmware drives two DC motors and no servos.
